newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany joins European shopping mall party - late. [CORRECTED 14:42 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Germany joins European shopping mall party - late. [CORRECTED 14:42 GMT]

text.p: Europe's largest retail complex opened on Thursday in Germany's Ruhr valley offering a "total shopping experience" meant to help transform the economic fortunes of the depressed industrial region.

Built in just two years on the site of an old steelworks, the 2.2 billion mark ($1.45 billion) CentrO mall symbolises belated efforts to restructure the ailing German economic juggernaut -- beset by soaring unemployment and fears its best years are past (corrects currencies).
"I hope this project will give a reviving impulse to the whole region, so badly shaken by unemployment," Johannes Rau, North Rhine-Westphalia premier, told an opening ceremony.

Germany is a latecomer to the U.S.-style shopping mall trend which has already peaked elsewhere in western Europe. Many markets are saturated and local officials have tightened planning rules to protect traditional city centres.

The British-built CentrO mall in Oberhausen has 220 shops, 50 eateries, nine cinemas, two hotels and an indoor stadium. It has 70,000 sq metres (750,000 sq ft) of floor space spread over a park of 830,000 sq metres (8.9 million sq ft).

Planned to employ 10,000 and billed as Europe's biggest in terms of total area, CentrO is still dwarfed by some U.S. malls. Its opening coincides with a mall construction slowdown in other European countries:
-- France has three complexes with space of over 100,000 sq metres, with the Belle Epine centre outside Paris the country's largest at 132,000 sq metres.
But the government, concerned about the rise of out-of-town shopping, last March lowered the ceiling for stores requiring special approval from 1,000 to 300 sq metres.
-- The largest of Britain's five big malls is Metro Centre near Newcastle with an area of 185,000 sq metres.

"Another six are in development. It is unlikely the government would give planning permission for more after the current crop are finished," said Clive Vaughan of retail analysts Verdict Research in London .

-- Traditional city shops have survived intact in Italy, where restrictive planning laws have kept the number of big shopping malls down to just eight. "Italy does not go in for huge malls at the moment," said Mauro Bussoni, spokesman for retail association Confesercenti.
-- Sweden has 30 smaller malls around Stockholm. Sales are rising but downtown centres are not under threat, said Rolk Karp of the wholesale and retail research institute.
-- Denmark's largest mall, City 2, in a Copenhagen suburb, was built during a 1970s shopping centre boom, but a surfeit of unrented space has largely reversed the trend since.

-- Austria's Shopping City Sued, outside Vienna, was opened in 1976 and has over 200 shops. But the shopping mall boom has peaked, marked by the recent redevelopment Vienna's main city shopping street, Mariahilferstrasse.

-- In Belgium and the Netherlands, the out-of-town shopping culture has not yet taken off and few malls have been built. "I think the inner cities will still be very important in Dutch retailing," said Patrick Manning of the Dutch Retail Council.

Parts of both Belgium and Holland fall within CentrO's catchment area 30 of million people living within two hours' drive. Analysts still expect CentrO project to do well despite initial resistance from the conservative German consumer.

"He would rather go to the supermarket round the corner than get in his car. But high prices, short shopping hours and a lack of choice will eventually drive him out of town," said Michael Wand, retail analyst for Paribas in Frankfurt.
No other super-malls are being planned in western Germany for now, possibly because of a wild boom-and-bust cycle of mall building in eastern Germany just after unification in 1990.
They would probably meet stiff resistance from high street retailers keen to defend their shops in the many pedestrian zones in the heart of Germany's cities.
Germany's retail association, protesting at the granting of state subsidies for CentrO, said the new consumer magnet would leave "scorched earth all around" and "strangle" city centres.
